{"id": "92:17/q07", "question": "Does this verse establish Abu Bakr's rank after the Prophet?", "turns_on": "Whether a verse about piety identifies an absolute personal rank and whether the reported referent is exclusive.", "positions": [{"id": "92:17/q07/p1", "position": "Abu Bakr is the community's best after the Prophet.", "reasons": "Al-Razi joins the most God-fearing here to the most honored in 49:13: visible piety reveals otherwise hidden rank. He says consensus narrows the candidate to Abu Bakr or Ali, then excludes Ali because of the Prophet's prior care, invoking 25:57. Al-Itqan reports this reasoning. Al-Biqa'i adds the promise of satisfaction and a report that God and believers accept Abu Bakr."}, {"id": "92:17/q07/p2", "position": "The description does not prove that one person is absolutely best of all people.", "reasons": "Tabataba'i rejects the absolute rank inference and the assertion that all Shia sources name Ali; al-Alusi describes the Imam's rank argument as disputable."}]}
{"id": "92:17/q08", "question": "How do the two apparent restrictions about Hell fit together?", "turns_on": "Whether 'only' yields a logical converse, whether ṣaly means any entry or severe torment, and whether the superlatives mark classes or exemplary figures.", "positions": [{"id": "92:17/q08/p1", "position": "The paired superlatives are rhetorical portraits of exemplary opponents, not strict exclusions of everyone else.", "reasons": "Al-Zamakhshari likens the Fire and Garden to places made for the leading disbeliever and believer; examples are Abu Jahl or Umayya and Abu Bakr. Al-Kashf approves. Al-Alusi prefers this after weighing alternatives, though he notes the Mu'tazilite premise about grave sinners. Islahi rejects a literal inference that only the extremes are damned or saved."}, {"id": "92:17/q08/p2", "position": "The earlier ṣaly is exceptionally severe burning, so other sinners may enter or receive lesser punishment.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Munir's lexical report likens ṣaly to placing an animal between layers of coals. Al-Alusi accepts this resolution; al-Baydawi and al-Biqa'i distinguish sinful believers' temporary entry from the wretched unbeliever's abiding fate."}, {"id": "92:17/q08/p3", "position": "Descriptive restriction has no valid converse: less pious people are not thereby condemned.", "reasons": "Al-Razi says al-Qadi himself rejects such implication and that it would wrongly send children and the insane to Hell. Al-Alusi gives this possible reply but finds the earlier 'only the most wretched' harder. Al-Jishumi says children and the insane are outside the warned audience. Islahi says the inference would equally and wrongly restrict salvation to only the most pious."}, {"id": "92:17/q08/p4", "position": "The two elatives name broad classes of wretched unbelievers and pious believers.", "reasons": "Abu Ubayda, quoted by al-Nasafi, and the generic readings use afʿal as an ordinary descriptor. Al-Alusi objects that this alone leaves sinful believers, poor pious people, children and the mentally ill difficult to place."}, {"id": "92:17/q08/p5", "position": "The indefinite 'a Fire' can denote one level of Hell rather than every level.", "reasons": "Al-Qadi proposes this; al-Zamakhshari objects that the following restriction still seems to exclude all but the most pious from that level. Al-Alusi also reports the broader apparent tension."}, {"id": "92:17/q08/p6", "position": "If sinners are not the most pious, the second restriction implies that they enter Hell.", "reasons": "Al-Qadi argues this from the converse. Al-Razi rejects the inference, citing children and the insane and al-Qadi's own view of implication."}, {"id": "92:17/q08/p7", "position": "Only the most wretched enter Hell, so less-wretched people are spared.", "reasons": "Islahi reports this inference; Abu Hurayra's hadith quoted by al-Alusi says only the wretched enter and describes one who neither obeys God nor refrains from sin for God. Al-Alusi says Sunnis read such reports alongside evidence that grave sinners may be punished. Al-Nasafi rejects the Murji'ite restriction of entry to unbelievers."}, {"id": "92:17/q08/p8", "position": "At Islam's beginning the contrast matched two actual groups: deniers and fully committed converts.", "reasons": "Ibn Ashur says the first converts did not commit major sins, so the promise supplies the converse to the warning. Islahi reads the contrast as Messenger rejecters and responsive believers rather than degrees within either group; a conclusive warning leaves rejecters no excuse."}]}
{"id": "92:17/q09", "question": "What qualities make this person God-fearing?", "turns_on": "Which traits the adjacent verses and reported exemplary acts attach to the title.", "positions": [{"id": "92:17/q09/p1", "position": "He avoids idolatry and sins, and purifies himself through sincere giving for God.", "reasons": "Al-Biqa'i speaks of a firm knowing faculty and peak piety; al-Wahidi reports Muqatil's sincere affirmation of God's oneness. Ibn Kathir calls him pure. Islahi connects heedfulness, judgment and cleansing wealth; Kuran Yolu traces taqwā to protection from danger and explains that giving seeks God's approval without repayment. The Study Quran notes charity purifies giver and wealth, with tazakkā related to zakāh. Corpus Coranicum calls the Lord's face a biblical metaphor."}, {"id": "92:17/q09/p2", "position": "He gives without settling a debt or repaying a favor, seeking God and His Messenger alone.", "reasons": "Tustari recounts Abu Bakr's answer about what he retained; Ibn Ata says the highest pious abandon the transient world. Al-Razi says a repayment earns no reward, whereas giving in response to God's command does. The Bilal reports say revelation answered a claim of prior favor."}, {"id": "92:17/q09/p3", "position": "He is the fortunate counterpart to the most wretched.", "reasons": "Qutb places the two figures against one another, drawing on verses 15–16."}]}
{"id": "92:17/q10", "question": "What inward state does the most God-fearing reach?", "turns_on": "Whether the piety is expressed as renunciation, union, or posthumous light.", "positions": [{"id": "92:17/q10/p1", "position": "The most pious abandons the transient world for God and His Messenger.", "reasons": "Tustari and Ibn Ata cite Abu Bakr's giving and his answer that he kept God and the Messenger; Ibn Ata calls ordinary pious people ascetics and the highest those who abandon the world entirely."}, {"id": "92:17/q10/p2", "position": "The absolutely God-fearing rejects all otherness and is absorbed in unity, escaping every level of fire.", "reasons": "Qashani contrasts this with stopping at attributes: such a person may be forgiven but remains veiled from the Essence's joy."}, {"id": "92:17/q10/p3", "position": "Good deeds, including night prayer, bring light after death.", "reasons": "Al-Biqa'i reports this as an interpretation of spiritual light becoming sensory light."}]}
{"id": "92:17/q11", "question": "How does the wording connect this verse with the surrounding passage and sura?", "turns_on": "Which surrounding verses or earlier Qur'anic wording the interpreter takes as the link.", "positions": [{"id": "92:17/q11/p1", "position": "It completes the sura's contrast of conduct and recompense for the saved and damned.", "reasons": "Bint al-Shati links the opening oaths over night, day and creation to divergent efforts and final fates. Corpus Coranicum describes two antitheses, a reversal of the earlier saved/damned order, the tie between ittaqā in verse 5 and atqā here, and the final stanza's inverted order of conduct and result. Islahi says verses 15–21 spell out both traits and rewards; Kuran Yolu notes the transition from the Fire warning to sincere giving and protection. Al-Alusi says the sura details the preceding sura's success and failure."}, {"id": "92:17/q11/p2", "position": "The phrase parallels 87:11 and recalls taqwā or ittaqā in verse 5.", "reasons": "Corpus Coranicum gives both the external parallel and the internal word link."}, {"id": "92:17/q11/p3", "position": "The promise that Abu Bakr will be pleased echoes the promise that God's gift satisfies the Prophet.", "reasons": "Al-Biqa'i uses this connection to describe Abu Bakr as closest in the community to the Prophet's station."}]}
{"id": "92:17/q12", "question": "What rhetorical contrast does al-atqā make with al-ashqā?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "92:17/q12/p1", "position": "The two labels directly oppose the damned and saved, with a near rhyme or near paronomasia.", "reasons": "Ibn Ashur names jinās muḍāriʿ and says the later relative clauses point to deeds causing each verdict. Corpus Coranicum says the moral opposition is named explicitly."}]}
{"id": "92:17/q13", "question": "What other grammatical observations occur in the verse's collected notes?", "turns_on": "Which of two separate general grammatical observations is being made.", "positions": [{"id": "92:17/q13/p1", "position": "A nominal circumstantial clause may omit wāw when its fronted predicate makes it closely resemble a single-object construction.", "reasons": "Al-Jurjani analyzes wajadtuhu ḥāḍirāhu al-jūd wa-l-karam: the verb takes one object, and fronting ḥāḍirāhu makes omission of wāw sound better than the reverse order."}, {"id": "92:17/q13/p2", "position": "Adjective agreement normally follows the preceding word's form; agreement by meaning is rarer.", "reasons": "Al-Zarkashi's Burhan states the form-versus-meaning rule for adjectives and similar constructions."}]}
{"id": "92:18/q01", "question": "Who is the Godfearing giver?", "turns_on": "Whether the named occasion limits the wording, and whether the Medinan palm story can be the occasion of an early Makkan sūra.", "positions": [{"id": "92:18/q01/p1", "position": "Abu Bakr.", "reasons": "Tustari calls him the truthful one, who abandoned the perishable for the everlasting; Thaʿlabi, Baghawi, and others connect the verse to his freeing perse

Kuranyolu and Study Quran report this as an occasion while allowing a general message."}, {"id": "92:18/q01/p2", "position": "Abu al-Dahdah.", "reasons": "Thaʿlabi and Qurtubi connect him to the donated date palm; Qurtubi contrasts him with its miserly owner. Study Quran recounts this as a Medinan report, but doubts it as the occasion if the sūra is early Makkan."}, {"id": "92:18/q01/p3", "position": "Ali.", "reasons": "Al-Razi reports the Shiʿi identification, linked to alms given while bowing in 5:55; they reject the Abu Bakr report."}, {"id": "92:18/q01/p4", "position": "Anyone who gives seeking purification; Abu Bakr can be one instance.", "reasons": "Ibn Ashur says an unusual named instance does not restrict general wording. Kuranyolu says the message and rulings remain general regardless of occasion. Study Quran's early Makkan dating favors a general condemnation and praise."}]}
{"id": "92:18/q02", "question": "What does يُؤْتِى convey as a word?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "92:18/q02/p1", "position": "Giving readily and generously.", "reasons": "Bint al-Shati compares a flood and a fruiting tree that yield readily; she cites 2:265, 13:35, 14:25, and 18:33. She says Quranic forms of zakat recur with giving, citing 23:4 and 24:37, 21:73, 4:162, 2:177, 9:11, 9:18, 24:56, 2:43, 2:83, 2:110, 2:277, 4:77, 9:5, 22:41, 22:78, 5:12, and 30:39."}, {"id": "92:18/q02/p2", "position": "Giving or spending wealth.", "reasons": "Alusi glosses the verb as giving and spending."}]}
{"id": "92:18/q03", "question": "Where or for what is the wealth given?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "92:18/q03/p1", "position": "It is spent in charity, obedience, and good causes, including help to the poor.", "reasons": "Baydawi, Biqai, and Alusi specify good causes; Nasafi specifies the poor. Ibn Kathir says obedience to God, purifying what God granted in religious and worldly life. Jishumi includes charity and other obedient acts. Qutb adds that giving is voluntary, without seeking thanks."}]}
{"id": "92:18/q04", "question": "Does the giving denote an obligation or voluntary good works?", "turns_on": "Whether the verse's giving is read as imposed alms or as freely chosen good works.", "positions": [{"id": "92:18/q04/p1", "position": "It includes fulfilling the wealth obligations God imposed, including obligatory alms.", "reasons": "Tabari says the obligations purify the giver of sins. Jishumi names charity and obligatory alms. Bint al-Shati describes religious zakat as obligatory wealth and says God's blessing and reward cause growth."}, {"id": "92:18/q04/p2", "position": "The apparent setting is recommended or voluntary giving.", "reasons": "Ibn Atiyya explicitly calls the apparent sense recommended works; Qutb describes the giver as acting voluntarily."}]}
{"id": "92:18/q05", "question": "What does مَالَهُۥ denote?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "92:18/q05/p1", "position": "Useful owned property and its yields; in some Arab usage, specifically date palms.", "reasons": "Ibn Ashur names livestock, land, private wells, and trees as generic māl. He says some Arabs, including Yathrib's people, used the word for date palms."}]}
{"id": "92:18/q06", "question": "Must the giver give all his wealth?", "turns_on": "The distinction between what the generic wording requires and what a report says one giver did.", "positions": [{"id": "92:18/q06/p1", "position": "No; the generic construct does not imply totality.", "reasons": "Ibn Ashur says māl in this construction is generic, so the verse does not require surrendering everything owned."}, {"id": "92:18/q06/p2", "position": "Abu Bakr spent all forty thousand he had.", "reasons": "Urwa's account in Thaʿlabi says he freed Bilal and others and gave away all forty thousand; this is a reported individual act, not a rule about the verse's grammar."}]}
{"id": "92:18/q07", "question": "What does يَتَزَكَّىٰ mean lexically?", "turns_on": "Whether the verb describes the giver's sought purity or the act of paying zakat.", "positions": [{"id": "92:18/q07/p1", "position": "To seek purification and growth in goodness.", "reasons": "Ibn Atiyya gives both purity and increase. Ibn Ashur defines tazakki as seeking zakāʾ, growth in goodness; Bint al-Shati traces growth to ripening fruit and explains nonphysical goodness and blessing, self-praise in 53:32, and refinement in 3:164 and 62:2. Corpus Coranicum compares 91:9 and 91:15."}, {"id": "92:18/q07/p2", "position": "To pay zakat or alms.", "reasons": "Kashshaf offers the verb form for giving zakat; Nasafi and Abu Hayyan also derive it from zakāh or tazkiya. Bint al-Shati says all 32 Quranic occurrences of the religious term zakat mean obligatory wealth, and compares 9:103 where wealth is purified; Study Quran notes the shared root."}]}
{"id": "92:18/q08", "question": "What purification does the giver seek?", "turns_on": "Which object or aspect of purification the commentators emphasize: standing before God, removal of sins, or the giver and wealth together.", "positions": [{"id": "92:18/q08/p1", "position": "Purity and growth before God, with His acceptance and pleasure rather than public praise.", "reasons": "Abu Ishaq, Wahidi, Baghawi, Kashshaf, Ibn al-Jawzi, Qurtubi, Nasafi, Abu Hayyan, Alusi, and Qutb reject ostentation and reputation. Qutb adds self-exaltation, repayment, and thanks; Ibn Ashur adds benefit and increased reward and contrasts idolaters' pride, display, mischief, and debauchery. Elmalili includes spiritual growth and prosperity. Corpus Coranicum says the longer portrait makes generosity ethical purification for the Lord's face, not repayment."}, {"id": "92:18/q08/p2", "position": "Cleansing himself from sins.", "reasons": "Tabari and Nahhas state this directly; Alusi offers it as an alternative to seeking pure, growing wealth before God."}, {"id": "92:18/q08/p3", "position": "Purifying both the person and the wealth God granted.", "reasons": "Ibn Kathir includes the self, wealth, and gifts in religion and worldly life. Islahi says believers spend to cleanse their wealth; Study Quran says charity purifies giver and wealth."}]}
{"id": "92:18/q09", "question": "What inward attachments are removed by this giving?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "92:18/q09/p1", "position": "Love of rivals, attachment to otherness, attention to anything besides God, and hidden shirk.", "reasons": "Qashani names each attachment as what the gift purges."}]}
{"id": "92:18/q10", "question": "How is يَتَزَكَّىٰ related grammatically to يُؤْتِى?", "turns_on": "Whether the imperfect states the giver's circumstance, substitutes for a preceding clause or verb, or depends on omitted purpose particles; objections concern case matching and the source of nominative inflection.", "positions": [{"id": "92:18/q10/p1", "position": "An accusative circumstantial clause describing the subject as he gives.", "reasons": "Jurjani says an affirmative imperfect circumstantial clause normally lacks wāw, citing this verse, 74:6, 7:186, and poetry. Abu Hayyan calls it usual and al-Zamakhshari's substitute strained; Bint al-Shati prefers it. Ibn Ashur says this parse conveys the giver's motive and increased reward."}, {"id": "92:18/q10/p2", "position": "A substitute for the relative clause, with no independent syntactic position.", "reasons": "Kashshaf, Baydawi, Nasafi, and others report or allow this. Alusi records the objection that the relative clause has no case to follow, and the response that correspondence can mean matching the presence or absence of case; al-Sayyid Isa defines a follower as a second item that would be inflected if inflectable. Abu Hayyan and Bint al-Shati call it strained."}, {"id": "92:18/q10/p3", "position": "The verb alone substitutes for the preceding verb.", "reasons": "Alusi reports this second substitution. Critics say its nominative is already explained by absence of a governor; the response allows a case to be intended despite an independent license, and al-Sayyid Isa states the follower test."}, {"id": "92:18/q10/p4", "position": "An implied purposive li-an precedes the verb; both lām and an are omitted.", "reasons": "Tabrisi invokes deletion of an with a line by Tarafa. Alusi reports that deleting lām then an permits a raised or subjunctive verb, illustrated by two transmitted readings of Tarafa's aḥḍur."}]}
{"id": "92:18/q11", "question": "How is يَتَزَكَّىٰ read?", "turns_on": "Whether the tāʾ of tazakkā remains pronounced or assimilates into zāy.", "positions": [{"id": "92:18/q11/p1", "position": "The common reading is yatazakkā, imperfect of tazakkā.", "reasons": "Abu Hayyan and al-Samin call it the majority or common reading."}, {"id": "92:18/q11/p2", "position": "Al-Hasan ibn Ali reads yazakkā, assimilating tāʾ into zāy.", "reasons": "Abu Hayyan, al-Samin, and Alusi attribute the assimilated form to al-Hasan ibn Ali ibn al-Hasan ibn Ali ibn Abi Talib; Alusi Full writes it يزكي."}]}
{"id": "92:18/q12", "question": "What does the giving teach about favors and repayment?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "92:18/q12/p1", "position": "The giver seeks God's reward without settling a favor owed to anyone.", "reasons": "Razi says repaying a benefactor merely settles a debt; reward follows acting on God's command. Ibn Kathir says Abu Bakr owed no one repayment although Arab leaders benefited from him. Qutb rejects thanks and repayment, and Kuranyolu says all blessings come from God. Corpus Coranicum links the ethical motive to seeking the Lord's face."}]}

Baghawi Full's list varies by omitting Zahra but says six more. Urwa says seven in

{"id": "92:18/q14", "question": "What did Abu Bakr say when advised to buy stronger protectors?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "92:18/q14/p1", "position": "He sought protection for himself, meaning a purpose other than a worldly defender.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Zubayr in Thaʿlabi says he pursued his own aim; Baghawi says protection for his own back, and Baghawi Full says protection precisely. Biqai's reports use a similar reply yet distinguish his purpose from buying a worldly defender. Study Quran phrases it as seeking no defense. The reported wording varies."}]}
{"id": "92:18/q15", "question": "How did Abu Bakr obtain Bilal's freedom?", "turns_on": "The reports differ on whether the payment was gold, an unnamed stronger enslaved man, or Nustas.", "positions": [{"id": "92:18/q15/p1", "position": "He bought Bilal with gold.", "reasons": "Aʿta from Ibn Abbas says Bilal endured torture, the Prophet reassured him, then Abu Bakr bought him with gold. Study Quran says the Prophet told Abu Bakr Bilal was tortured for God; idolaters later alleged an earlier favor prompted the purchase."}, {"id": "92:18/q15/p2", "position": "He exchanged a stronger enslaved man for Bilal and freed him.", "reasons": "Hisham ibn Urwa says Abu Bakr challenged Umayya's torture before the exchange; Baghawi Full also reports the exchange."}, {"id": "92:18/q15/p3", "position": "He traded Nustas, a wealthy enslaved man who refused Islam, for Bilal.", "reasons": "Saʿid ibn al-Musayyib says the emancipation was solely for God and God promised repayment in the hereafter."}, {"id": "92:18/q15/p4", "position": "He bought Bilal from Umayya; the consideration is unspecified.", "reasons": "Biqai locates the purchase amid midday torture and Bilal's repeated 'One, One'; idolaters claimed repayment of a past favor, which revelation refuted."}]}
{"id": "92:18/q16", "question": "What did Bilal endure before he was freed?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "92:18/q16/p1", "position": "Umayya tortured him for his monotheistic faith while he affirmed God's oneness.", "reasons": "Ibn Ishaq puts the torture under a boulder in Mecca's noonday heat and quotes 'Ahad, Ahad.' Aʿta adds the Prophet's reassurance; Study Quran's account says Bilal had desecrated Kaʿbah idols and the Prophet promised the One would save him."}]}
{"id": "92:18/q17", "question": "What happened in the palm tree account associated with this passage?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "92:18/q17/p1", "position": "Abu al-Dahdah bought a disputed palm and gave it for a poor neighbor after its owner refused the Prophet's Paradise offer.", "reasons": "Thaʿlabi describes fruit falling into a neighbor's yard; Study Quran says the owner snatched dates from poor children, refused the offer, and Abu al-Dahdah paid forty palms before the Prophet transferred the tree. Qurtubi maps miser and giver to the sūra's contrasting outcomes. Study Quran doubts this is the occasion if the sūra is early Makkan."}]}
{"id": "92:18/q18", "question": "What is reported about Zahra's sight?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "92:18/q18/p1", "position": "Her sight returned after she denied that idols had power over her blindness.", "reasons": "Baghawi, Baghawi Full, and Biqai say Quraysh attributed her impaired sight to idols; she rejected their power and recovered. The accounts vary in naming her Zahra or Umm Umays."}]}
{"id": "92:18/q19", "question": "What other reports illustrate Abu Bakr's devotion or standing?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "92:18/q19/p1", "position": "He told the Prophet he had kept God and His Messenger for himself.", "reasons": "Tustari reports the Prophet's question about what Abu Bakr retained after giving."}, {"id": "92:18/q19/p2", "position": "The Prophet hoped Abu Bakr would be called from every gate of Paradise.", "reasons": "Ibn Kathir Full reports a saying that gates call those who spend two kinds of wealth in God's path; asked whether anyone receives every call, the Prophet named Abu Bakr as hoped for."}, {"id": "92:18/q19/p3", "position": "The Prophet said God and believers would accept only Abu Bakr.", "reasons": "Biqai treats the report as supporting Abu Bakr's unique closeness to the Prophet and his contrast with the worst unbeliever."}, {"id": "92:18/q19/p4", "position": "Bilal later became the first caller to prayer and one of the Prophet's treasurers.", "reasons": "Study Quran supplies this aftermath of his freeing."}]}
{"id": "92:18/q20", "question": "How does this verse connect with the sūra's contrasting figures and outcomes?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "92:18/q20/p1", "position": "The giver's conduct contrasts with denial, hoarding, and the fire; purification leads toward rescue and satisfaction.", "reasons": "Biqai contrasts cleansing bad traits with denial in 92:16. Bint al-Shati contrasts the miser's useless wealth in 92:11 with the gift in 92:18 and frames both by the opening oath. Islahi describes Quraysh's warning, believers' response, fire and protection. Kuranyolu links 92:14 with 92:17–20. Corpus Coranicum sees the two antitheses of conduct and recompense in 5–13 and 14–21."}, {"id": "92:18/q20/p2", "position": "The final stanza reverses and mirrors the earlier portrayal of saved and damned.", "reasons": "Corpus Coranicum says the blessed outer sections share ittaqā in 92:5 and atqā in 92:17; earlier behavior precedes outcome, whereas final warning and promise precede conduct. Its longer portrait of the pious clarifies ethical purification and the Lord's face."}, {"id": "92:18/q20/p3", "position": "The promise of Abu Bakr's satisfaction parallels God's promise to satisfy the Prophet.", "reasons": "Biqai says Abu Bakr is the closest in the community to the Prophet's station; the report of God's and believers' acceptance supports this."}, {"id": "92:18/q20/p4", "position": "The sūra's wealth motif suits emphatic wording of God's ownership.", "reasons": "Samarrai says a lām of emphasis on divine ownership fits the repeated concern with wealth and possession; he contrasts 53:25, where that wealth context is absent."}]}
{"id": "92:18/q21", "question": "What rhetorical work does the contrast around this verse perform?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "92:18/q21/p1", "position": "Reciprocal omission lets the denier's opposite and giver's opposite be understood.", "reasons": "Biqai calls this ḥatbāk: first naming denial implies its opposite for the pious; later naming giving implies its opposite for the denier."}, {"id": "92:18/q21/p2", "position": "The relative descriptions make conduct the cause of each outcome.", "reasons": "Ibn Ashur says clauses describing most wretched and most pious indicate why each receives the stated fate."}]}
{"id": "92:18/q22", "question": "What grammatical principle applies to agreement in the verse's modifying construction?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "92:18/q22/p1", "position": "Agreement normally follows the preceding word's form; agreement by meaning is less common.", "reasons": "Burhan states this rule for adjectives and similar constructions."}]}
{"id": "93:6/q01", "question": "What does the opening question do?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "93:6/q01/p1", "position": "It expects assent, emphatically affirming the established favor and reminding the Prophet of it.", "reasons": "Al-Burhān says a report interrogative presses an already known admission, cannot be formed with hal according to Abū al-Fatḥ, and can coordinate with an affirmative clause (94:1; 105:2). Al-Ālūsī describes the hamza as negating the negation. Ibn ʿĀshūr calls it confirmatory and pictures a distressed person met with aid."}]}
{"id": "93:6/q02", "question": "How does 'find' work here?", "turns_on": "Whether wajada denotes knowledge with two objects, encounter with a circumstantial accusative, or a figurative act of selection; literal discovery of new information is rejected for God.", "positions": [{"id": "93:6/q02/p1", "position": "It means know, taking 'you' and 'orphan' as two objects.", "reasons": "Al-Naḥḥās allows seeing or knowing with two objects; al-Zamakhsharī, al-Rāzī and al-Nasafī explicitly parse two accusatives. Elmalılı notes that creaturely finding follows absence or ignorance."}, {"id": "93:6/q02/p2", "position": "It means find or encounter; 'you' is its object and 'orphan' describes the circumstance.", "reasons": "Al-Bayḍāwī permits this alongside the two-object analysis. Ibn ʿĀshūr prefers the one-object construction for all three favor verses. Al-Biqāʿī takes finding as encounter followed by care. Al-Ālūsī allows it only figuratively of God, whose knowledge precedes all events."}, {"id": "93:6/q02/p3", "position": "Finding figuratively expresses God's choosing the Prophet from creation.", "reasons": "Elmalılı prefers istifāʾ: finding a rare valuable object images selection, repeated across the three verses."}, {"id": "93:6/q02/p4", "position": "It could mean bringing the Prophet into existence.", "reasons": "Elmalılı explicitly calls this possible but nonstandard."}, {"id": "93:6/q02/p5", "position": "The word foregrounds inward reassurance and belongs to a family of words for existence, knowledge, ecstasy and possession.", "reasons": "Bint al-Shāṭiʾ calls it a heart verb that attends to the Prophet's inner state. Elmalılı traces wājid to existence, finding, ecstasy and wealth; God possesses existence, knowledge, power and wealth."}]}

{"id": "93:6/q04", "question": "What does 'orphan' mean here?", "turns_on": "Whether yatīm carries its ordinary paternal-loss sense, the pearl metaphor, or a spiritual/allegorical sense.", "positions": [{"id": "93:6/q04/p1", "position": "A child whose father died before puberty, as Muhammad's father did.", "reasons": "Al-Māwardī, al-Ālūsī and Ibn ʿĀshūr define it by paternal death; al-Rāghib, cited by Bint al-Shāṭiʾ, adds the limit of puberty. Several notes stress that both parents eventually died. Bint al-Shāṭiʾ says Quranic contexts associate orphans with poverty, exposed property and oppression (2:83; 4:10; 89:17; 107:2, among others), and eleven passages pair orphanhood with poverty."}, {"id": "93:6/q04/p2", "position": "It means unmatched and peerless, like a unique pearl.", "reasons": "The pearl expression is cited by al-Māwardī, Mujāhid and others; the referent is unmatched honor and virtue among Quraysh, or potentially all creation in al-Ālūsī's suggested improvement. Elmalılı treats the sense as an additional rhetorical echo. Al-Zamakhsharī calls the interpretation inventive or eccentric; Abū Ḥayyān, al-Ālūsī and Bint al-Shāṭiʾ dismiss it."}, {"id": "93:6/q04/p3", "position": "It means solitary, and God placed him among companions.", "reasons": "Al-Tustarī explains yatīm as solitary rather than identifying it with paternal loss."}, {"id": "93:6/q04/p4", "position": "It signifies the solitary soul veiled by its own qualities from the true father, the Holy Spirit.", "reasons": "Al-Qāshānī says divine care and education restore the soul, with a fatherly guardian teaching and purifying it."}, {"id": "93:6/q04/p5", "position": "It refers allegorically to lacking a teacher.", "reasons": "ʿIṣām al-Dīn pairs this with lacking knowledge and a community needing guidance; al-Ālūsī calls the threefold allegory strained."}]}
{"id": "93:6/q05", "question": "What sequence of losses and guardianship do the reports give?", "turns_on": "The mother's age is given as two, six or eight; the father's death is placed before birth or shortly afterward.", "positions": [{"id": "93:6/q05/p1", "position": "His father died before his birth; his mother when he was six; his grandfather when he was eight; then Abu Talib cared for him.", "reasons": "Ibn Shihāb says ʿAbd Allāh died while seeking dates in Yathrib for ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib; al-Ālūsī and Elmalılı say Muhammad was a six-month fetus. Ibn Kathīr reports the six- and eight-year ages; Rāzī's historians and the full account agree. Al-Kāshshāf instead gives his mother's age as eight; other reports give two."}, {"id": "93:6/q05/p2", "position": "His father died before birth; his mother died when he was eight; Abu Talib then raised him.", "reasons": "Al-Kashshāf says the father died when Muhammad was a six-month fetus. Abū Ḥayyān repeats this chronology. Al-Biqāʿī and al-Ṭabrisī say the grandfather died when Muhammad was eight, with al-Ṭabrisī giving two rather than eight for his mother's death."}, {"id": "93:6/q05/p3", "position": "His father died before birth or soon after, his mother at two, and his grandfather at eight.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabrisī and al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī give two for the mother's death; al-Ṭabrisī allows the father's death shortly after birth."}, {"id": "93:6/q05/p4", "position": "His father may have died shortly after his birth.", "reasons": "Ibn Kathīr reports this as an alternative; Ibn ʿĀshūr likewise allows death very early in infancy."}, {"id": "93:6/q05/p5", "position": "The notes establish parental loss and succession of grandfather and uncle without fixing all ages.", "reasons": "Al-Māwardī describes care first by ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib, then Abū Ṭālib. ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿAmr stresses the loss of both parents."}]}
{"id": "93:6/q06", "question": "How did God shelter the Prophet?", "turns_on": "Whether shelter names a home and guardians, later companions, direct divine nurture, a nurse, or shelter extended to others through him.", "positions": [{"id": "93:6/q06/p1", "position": "He provided human guardians, especially Abu Talib, who raised, supported and protected him.", "reasons": "Muqātil and many others name Abū Ṭālib; al-Māwardī and al-Ṭabrisī include ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib first. Al-Farrāʾ says divine contentment relieved need for Abū Ṭālib without wealth. Ibn Kathīr says the uncle defended him despite remaining an idolater, and the Anṣār sheltered him after the uncle died. Qutb says God inclined hearts to care for him. Study Quran adds Khadīja as refuge; Islahi compares Moses' providential upbringing and cites 89:17 and 107:2."}, {"id": "93:6/q06/p2", "position": "He gave him a home and place to dwell.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī leaves the human guardian unspecified. Ibn Kathīr details the later Anṣār's defense and fighting for him after Abū Ṭālib's death."}, {"id": "93:6/q06/p5", "position": "He sheltered him in intimate divine care and selected him for the message.", "reasons": "Al-Māwardī and al-Ṭabrisī attach this to the peerless-person reading; al-Qushayrī says God nurtured him to an intimate station none shared. Elmalılı speaks of sheltering his heart; al-Qāshānī adds spiritual education."}, {"id": "93:6/q06/p6", "position": "He sheltered the Prophet through a wet nurse who came to love him.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī reports that wet nurses initially refused him, but blessing through his companionship changed the nurse's heart; he prefers the ordinary orphaned-child account."}, {"id": "93:6/q06/p7", "position": "He made the Prophet himself a refuge for orphans and protector of people.", "reasons": "Al-Māwardī reverses the image: one who had been cared for became caretaker. Ibn ʿAṭāʾ similarly says God shelters orphans, guides the lost and enriches the needy through him; al-Sāmarāʾī says shelter reaches others through or for him."}]}
{"id": "93:6/q07", "question": "What does āwā mean in this verse?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "93:6/q07/p1", "position": "It means to gather someone into a dwelling, protection or care.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī defines sheltering as joining one thing to another; Elmalılı as gathering and lodging. Ibn ʿĀshūr gives the literal root sense of returning to a dwelling, figuratively sponsorship and meeting needs; he says God developed the Prophet's understanding and character despite orphanhood. Bint al-Shāṭiʾ says fourteen Quranic uses convey haven or refuge and that the open verb implies safety from social and psychological harms rather than restoring his father or riches."}]}
{"id": "93:6/q08", "question": "How is fa-āwā read, and what can the alternate form mean?", "turns_on": "Whether the verb is quadriliteral or triliteral, and whether the shorter verb is taken as sheltering/refuge or mercy.", "positions": [{"id": "93:6/q08/p1", "position": "The common reading has the transitive quadriliteral fa-āwā, 'He sheltered.'", "reasons": "Abū Ḥayyān and al-Samīn contrast the majority's quadriliteral with Abū al-Ashhab's triliteral. {"id": "93:6/q09", "question": "Why is the object of 'sheltered' unspoken?", "turns_on": "Whether the omitted object simply supplies 'you' from context or deliberately broadens the beneficiaries.", "positions": [{"id": "93:6/q09/p1", "position": "The understood object is 'you'; omission is concise and preserves the verse endings.", "reasons": "Al-Farrāʾ, al-Thaʿlabī, al-Ālūsī and Ibn ʿĀshūr apply the same account to guided and enriched. {"id": "93:6/q14", "question": "How do Sūrat al-Ḍuḥā and Sūrat al-Sharḥ relate?", "turns_on": "Whether shared favor language outweighs the distinction between distress and expanded comfort.", "positions": [{"id": "93:6/q14/p1", "position": "Both recall divine favors, with Sūrat 93 addressing external needs and Sūrat 94 spiritual relief.", "reasons": "Study Quran says 94:1 repeats the interrogative pattern of 93:6, also implied in 93:7–8; both reassure, while 94 adds exertion and turning to God."}, {"id": "93:6/q14/p2", "position": "They may be counted as one sūrah because both enumerate favors.", "reasons": "Bint al-Shāṭiʾ reports this view, comparing shelter for the orphan with expansion of the breast."}, {"id": "93:6/q14/p3", "position": "The two openings describe different states and should not be equated.", "reasons": "Bursevī rejects an unidentified comparison: the first sūrah depicts distress from unbelievers, the second an opened breast and comfort."}]}
{"id": "93:6/q15", "question": "What does the report of the Prophet's request for other prophets' gifts say?", "turns_on": "Whether the miracle-comparison narrative is plausible for a prophet and whether its response is favor or reproach.", "positions": [{"id": "93:6/q15/p1", "position": "God answered his comparison by enumerating shelter, guidance, provision and further blessings, and the Prophet affirmed them.", "reasons": "Versions mention Abraham, Moses, David, Solomon, wind, fire, friendship, raised remembrance, the opened breast, removed burden, and 2:285–286. {"id": "93:6/q16", "question": "What occasion or pause is associated with the sūrah's revelation?", "turns_on": "The notes give different triggers, durations and reconstructions of the revelation pause.", "positions": [{"id": "93:6/q16/p1", "position": "Jewish questions followed by a promised answer without 'if God wills' preceded a pause.", "reasons": "Al-Thaʿlabī lists questions about Dhū al-Qarnayn, the Cave Companions and the Spirit."}, {"id": "93:6/q16/p2", "position": "A puppy in the house prevented Gabriel's entry.", "reasons": "Al-Jishumī reports Gabriel's statement that angels do not enter a house with a dog or image."}, {"id": "93:6/q16/p3", "position": "A cut finger, a recited couplet and Umm Jamīl's taunt preceded a short pause.", "reasons": "Jundub ibn Sufyān says revelation stopped two or three nights;
